 SoCal storm timeline: Back-to-back systems bring rain, high surf through Sunday
 By Alexa Mae Asperin FOX 11 Weather Published  November 11, 2026 9:52 AM PST Share
 Copy Link 
 Email 
 Facebook 
 Twitter 
 LinkedIn 
 Reddit 
 Published  November 11, 2026 9:52 AM PST Weather Forecast for Thursday, Nov. 12 
 The latest forecast and air quality conditions for the greater Los Angeles area, including beaches, valleys and desert regions. 
 The Brief
 Two consecutive Pacific storm systems will end Southern California's warm spell, bringing widespread rain and gusty winds starting late Thursday evening. 
 A High Surf Advisory takes effect at 2 p.m. Friday through Tuesday, with breaking waves peaking at 7 to 12 feet on Saturday and causing coastal flooding risks. 
 While weekend totals are projected at a quarter-inch to 1 inch, exact rainfall amounts for a potential mid-week storm are uncertain. 
 LOS ANGELES - Dry weather across Southern California will come to an end late Thursday evening as consecutive Pacific storm systems move into the region, triggering a sharp drop in temperatures, widespread rain, and hazardous coastal surf lasting into next week, according to the National Weather Service.
 What we know:
 The region is transitioning out of unseasonably warm conditions—which saw highs in the upper 70s to around 90 degrees—as high pressure weakens and Thursday's high temperatures drop 5 to 10 degrees compared to Wednesday. 
 Highs on Friday and Saturday are expected to settle into the 60s to low 70s alongside gusty southwest to northwest winds, according to the NWS. 
 Rain chances
 Overall chances for widespread rain sit above 90%, with most areas of Los Angeles and Orange counties expected to receive between a quarter-inch and 1 inch of total rainfall from the two systems, and locally higher amounts possible on mountain slopes and in thunderstorms.
 Hourly rainfall rates are expected to remain at or below a quarter-inch per hour in most areas, though forecasters note a 20% to 30% chance of localized rates reaching up to a half-inch per hour, meaning significant rain-related flooding is not anticipated. 
 There is also a slight chance of thunderstorms late Thursday and Friday, with the best chances occurring in Orange County and areas to the south.
 Dangerous rip currents, high surf
 Along the coast, a Beach Hazards Statement is in effect for the Malibu coast and Los Angeles County beaches through Friday afternoon due to dangerous rip currents and elevated surf, followed by a High Surf Advisory from 2 p.m. Friday until 3 p.m. Tuesday. 
 A large west-to-northwest swell will bring breaking waves of 4 to 7 feet on Friday, increasing to 7 to 12 feet on Saturday before declining to 6 to 9 feet from Sunday through Tuesday. 
 Combined with morning high tides peaking between 7.0 and 7.4 feet, this swell will bring dangerous rip currents, strong longshore currents, sneaker waves, and large shore break, threatening west- to northwest-facing beaches with significant beach erosion and shallow flooding of low-lying walkways, parking lots, and roads near high tide, particularly on Saturday morning, the NWS stated. 
 Timeline:
 Rain chances will increase after midnight in Los Angeles County late Thursday night, spreading across the region overnight before dawn on Friday.
 Scattered showers are expected primarily on Friday morning before tapering off after sunrise, though isolated showers may linger throughout the day.
 A second, more widespread round of rain associated with a frontal passage will move in late Friday afternoon or evening and continue into Saturday morning before clearing from west to east. Sunday will bring a brief dry break with daytime highs settling in the mid-60s to low 70s.
 What they're saying:
 NWS forecasters emphasized that the back-to-back systems will ensure broad coverage across the region without causing major rain-related disruptions. "Our next weather system is rapidly approaching," forecasters noted as the pattern shifts, adding, "Any areas that don't get wet Friday morning should get wet Friday night."
 Regarding the second wave of storms, forecasters stated, "Peak rain rates will be about the same so still not expecting any significant impacts." 
 Looking ahead to next week, the agency added, "Pattern-wise, the ‘storm train’ is expected to continue with one storm impacting the area Sunday night through Tuesday then another system during the day on Wednesday/Wednesday night."
 What you can do:
 If you are driving and encounter standing water on coastal streets, follow posted warnings and never drive around barricades or through flooded roads.
 Residents should also secure outdoor patio furniture or belongings exposed to surf and rain, and anyone with outdoor weekend plans should prepare for wet weather.
 Beachgoers are urged to remain out of the water or stay near occupied lifeguard towers, stay off rock jetties, and remain vigilant against sneaker waves, heavy shore breaks, and strong rip currents.
 What's next:
 Following Sunday’s brief dry spell, the "storm train" will bring another colder and faster-moving storm system into the area from Sunday night through Tuesday. 
 A third disturbance is projected to follow during the day on Wednesday or Wednesday night into Thursday, keeping cooler, unsettled conditions in place across Southern California through the middle of next week.
 The Source: This report is based on information provided by the National Weather Service. City News Service contributed.
